abstentions: Whether the surface language grammar permits a binder or let-bound name to shadow a component state or const name (determines whether claims 1 and 2 triggers are reachable or latent)
Whether the intended scoping semantics is local-binding-wins for shadowed names (determines the correct behavior and whether the observed qualification split is a defect or an intentional rule)

finding.description: rewrite_lvalue (687-698) routes LValue::Var and LValue::Index names through rewrite_state_name (700-706), which prefixes any name in component.names.state without consulting bound; bound is applied only to the Index sub-expression via rewrite_expr, never to the variable name itself. This is asymmetric with rewrite_statement's ForAll arm (670-683), which clones bound and inserts the binder before rewriting the body, and with rewrite_expr's Var arm (711-717), which guards qualification on !bound.contains(&name). Effect: within a ForAll (or Quantified/Aggregate) body whose binder name matches a component state name, an assignment or index target to that name is still prefixed to alias.x by rewrite_state_name while the identical name in the rvalue is left bare by rewrite_expr, producing alias.x := f(x) instead of the intended x := f(x). Reachability caveat: whether the surface grammar permits a binder to shadow a component state name is not established in the available projections; if shadowing is illegal, this asymmetry is latent rather than triggerable. The downstream kernel behavior for the mixed qualification is not in the projections, so the kernel-corruption consequence is inferred from the immediate qualification split rather than observed.
finding.title: Lvalue rewrite ignores the bound set, creating asymmetric qualification between lvalue and rvalue for shadowed names

decisions.reason: The structural asymmetry is confirmed verbatim in source: rewrite_lvalue (687-698) routes both LValue::Var and LValue::Index names through rewrite_state_name (700-706), which qualifies on component.names.state without consulting bound, while bound is applied only to the Index sub-expression via rewrite_expr. This is asymmetric with the ForAll arm (670-683), which extends bound before rewriting the body, and with rewrite_expr's Var arm (711-717), which guards on !bound.contains(&name). The critic confirms the mechanism but correctly notes that the trigger's reachability (whether the surface grammar permits a binder to shadow a state name) and the downstream 'corrupts the kernel' consequence are not established in any projection. The original overstates certainty on both counts; the finding is revised to separate the source-supported structural defect from the inferential trigger-reachability and downstream-consequence claims.

finding.description: rewrite_action_items (609-631) processes each ActionItem independently via .map with the same immutable bound reference; the Let arm (623-625) rewrites only the initializer expression and never inserts the bound name into bound. This contrasts with rewrite_binder (844-855), Expr::Quantified (796-802), and Expr::Aggregate (810-816), which all clone bound and insert the binder name before rewriting the body. The .map structure makes per-item bound extension impossible without restructuring the function, and Let is an ActionItem rather than a Statement, so there is no other path that would add its name to bound. Effect: if a let-bound name matches a component state or const name, a subsequent item's rvalue reference to that name is still rewritten by rewrite_expr's Var arm (711-717) to alias.name (the state/const) because !bound.contains(&name) still holds, rather than resolving to the local binding. Reachability and intent caveats: whether the surface grammar permits a let name to shadow a state/const name is not established in the projections; whether the intended scoping semantics is local-binding-wins is an interpretation rather than a projected fact; and the encoding of the subsequent reference as Expr::Var is assumed from the description rather than shown in a projection.
finding.title: Let arm in rewrite_action_items does not extend bound, unlike all other binder forms

decisions.reason: The structural defect is confirmed in source: rewrite_action_items (609-631) uses .map, so every item is transformed against the same immutable bound with no threading between items, and the Let arm (623-625) rewrites only the initializer without inserting the name into bound. This contrasts with rewrite_binder (844-855), Expr::Quantified (796-802), and Expr::Aggregate (810-816), which all clone bound and insert the binder. The Let arm is the only action-level binder that does not extend bound, and the .map structure makes extension impossible without changing the function. The critic confirms the mechanism but correctly notes that the trigger's reachability (whether a let name may shadow a state/const name), the encoding of the subsequent reference (assumed Expr::Var), and the intended semantics (local-shadow-wins) are all inferential. The finding is revised to separate the source-supported structural defect from the inferential trigger-reachability and semantics-intent claims.

finding.description: rewrite_expr ends in `other => other` (840) and rewrite_type ends in `other => other` (589): any Expr/TypeExpr variant not explicitly enumerated is returned unchanged, with no qualification of embedded identifiers and no compile-time exhaustiveness error. Trigger: any fall-through variant carrying unqualified state/const/type names (including variants added later) yields unresolvable references in the lowered kernel; the catch-all makes the omission silent. Expr::Call likewise leaves its name unqualified (742-749), which is sound only if call names are always global.
finding.title: Non-exhaustive rewrite_expr/rewrite_type catch-alls (other => other) silently pass unhandled variants through without qualification

decisions.reason: The structural facts are directly in source: rewrite_expr terminates in other => other (840) and rewrite_type terminates in other => other (589), so any Expr/TypeExpr variant not enumerated is returned unchanged with embedded identifiers unqualified and no compile-time exhaustiveness error. The catch-all arm makes the match compile regardless of new variants, so the latent-hazard reading is correct and is the claim's core, which holds by construction. The claim is properly hedged ('any fall-through variant … including variants added later'), so it does not overreach by asserting a present-day trigger. The critic confirms the structural mechanism and notes only that the present-day instantiation cannot be confirmed from the projections (full enum definitions are absent) and that the downstream 'unresolvable reference' consequence is inferred. The Expr::Call observation (742-749) is correctly noted as sound only under the condition that call names are always global. The finding is retained as stated.

information_loss: Full Expr/TypeExpr/LValue/ActionItem/Binder enum definitions reside in the AST module, not in any available card, so no current-variant fall-through can be confirmed for claim 3 and the complete set of binder forms cannot be enumerated for claims 1 and 2
Surface-language binding rules (shadowing legality) are not in any projection, leaving reachability of claims 1 and 2 undetermined
No runtime trace, kernel semantics, or downstream name-resolution behavior is available, so all consequences describing kernel corruption or unresolvable references are inferred
summary: Three findings in compose.rs name-qualification rewrite. Two are real structural asymmetries in how bound is threaded — the lvalue path ignores bound for names while the rvalue path honors it, and the Let arm never extends bound unlike all other binder forms; both are confirmed in source but their triggers depend on shadowing legality that is absent from the projections. The third (non-exhaustive catch-all arms) is a confirmed latent hazard, properly hedged. All three share the same projection gap: AST enum definitions, surface-language binding rules, and downstream kernel semantics are unavailable, so trigger-reachability and consequence claims are inferred rather than observed.
